ML-015: Creoleana was written by a white Barbadian who lived through the era of slavery, and it looks back fondly on island society in those years. Its love story takes place in a world built on the forced labour of enslaved Africans, whose own voices the book largely leaves out. We include it because it is one of the earliest Barbadian novels, but it is a view from one side of a deeply unequal society.
ML-146: James Grainger was a Scottish doctor who settled on St Kitts, married into a planter family and lived within the plantation economy. His best-known poem, The Sugar-Cane, includes advice on buying and managing enslaved people. This ballad of two lovers comes from that world, and its tenderness sits uneasily beside the cruelty that sustained it.
ML-168: John Gabriel Stedman was a soldier sent to Suriname to fight people who had escaped slavery. His account of Joanna, an enslaved woman, is often read as a love story, but he wrote it as a man with power over her, and her own view of their relationship was never recorded. It is included as an important, and troubling, record of love under slavery.
ML-110: Paul et Virginie was written by a French author who had lived on the island when it was a French colony worked by enslaved people. He criticised slavery in his other writing, yet the story's island idyll still depends on enslaved characters who serve in the background. It became one of the most widely read love stories of its age, and its picture of colonial life should be read with that history in mind.
ML-001: Rābiʿa Balkhi lived in Balkh in the tenth century and is remembered as one of the first women to write poetry in Persian. Legend says her brother killed her for loving a servant named Baktash; her story mixes history and legend, and her shrine in Balkh is still visited today.
ML-002: Naim Frashëri wrote when Albania was still part of the Ottoman Empire and books in Albanian were restricted. He became the leading poet of the Albanian national awakening, and his verse, often printed abroad, mixes love, nature and a mystical faith.
ML-003: Emir Abd al-Qadir led Algerian resistance to the French conquest from 1832 until he surrendered in 1847. He was imprisoned in France and spent his last decades in exile in Damascus as a scholar, Sufi and poet, so his love poems sit alongside a life shaped by war and exile.
ML-005: Cordeiro da Matta wrote in Luanda when Angola was a Portuguese colony, and is counted among the first Angolan poets. He also compiled a Kimbundu dictionary and collected proverbs, part of an early effort to value African languages under colonial rule; the woman in this poem answers in Kimbundu.
ML-196: Alfonsina Storni came to Argentina from Switzerland as a child and became one of the boldest voices in Latin American poetry, writing as a working single mother in Buenos Aires. Her early books spoke frankly of women's desire at a time when that was rare and often criticised.
ML-008: Sayat-Nova was an eighteenth-century minstrel who sang at the court of King Erekle II in Tbilisi, a city where Armenian, Georgian and Azerbaijani cultures met. He composed in all three languages; tradition says he was killed when Persian forces sacked the city in 1795.
ML-197: Henry Kendall was one of the first poets born in the Australian colonies, and set out to write about their landscapes in their own right. His life was marked by poverty and grief, which colour this memory of first love; the colonies he celebrated were built on land taken from Aboriginal peoples.
ML-198: Ada Christen grew up poor in Vienna and worked as an actress before she published her first poems. Lieder einer Verlorenen ('Songs of a Lost Woman', 1868) shocked readers with its frank picture of poverty and women's lives, and this poem's distrust of fine words comes from that experience.
ML-199: Khurshidbanu Natavan, daughter of the last khan of Karabakh, was one of the best-known women poets of the nineteenth-century Caucasus, then under Russian rule. In her home city of Shusha she led a literary circle and paid for the town's first water supply.
ML-013: Abu al-Bahr al-Khatti lived around 1600, when Bahrain was fought over by Portugal and Safavid Persia, which took the islands in 1602. He was a well-travelled scholar of the Gulf whose Arabic verse moves easily between gardens, faith and love.
ML-014: Mahua is one of the ballads sung for generations in the Mymensingh region of eastern Bengal. The scholar Dinesh Chandra Sen had them collected from village singers and published in the 1920s, preserving a rural tradition in which women often choose love against family and custom.
ML-016: Maksim Bahdanovich wrote when Belarus was part of the Russian Empire, and writing in Belarusian was itself a statement of identity. He published one book in his lifetime and died of tuberculosis in 1917, aged 25; this poem later became a much-loved song.
ML-200: Émile Verhaeren was a Flemish Belgian who wrote in French, best known for poems about cities and industry. Les Heures claires (1896) is different: a quiet sequence written for his wife, the painter Marthe Massin, celebrating a calm, shared love.
ML-021: Ricardo Jaimes Freyre was a leader of modernismo, the movement that renewed Spanish-language poetry around 1900. Born to Bolivian parents in Tacna, he spent much of his life in Argentina and later served Bolivia as a diplomat and minister.
ML-022: Aleksa Šantić wrote in Mostar soon after Austria-Hungary took Bosnia over from the Ottoman Empire. Emina, about a Muslim girl in a garden, became a beloved sevdalinka, the region's traditional love song, sung by people of every community in a city later divided by war.
ML-201: Olavo Bilac published this sonnet in 1888, the year slavery was finally abolished in Brazil and a year before the empire became a republic. He was the leading poet of Brazil's Parnassian movement, admired for polished, musical sonnets like this one.
ML-202: Mara Belcheva's husband, a finance minister, was killed in an assassination attempt aimed at the prime minister in 1891. She later became the companion of the poet Pencho Slaveykov, and published her Sonnets in 1925, in her fifties, as love poems of a full and hard life.
ML-203: This poem is set at Grand Pré in Nova Scotia, the heart of Acadie. In 1755 British authorities expelled the French-speaking Acadians from these lands, and the tidal flats of Grand Pré have carried that memory of loss ever since, which deepens the poem's sense of absence.
ML-204: Gabriela Mistral was a rural schoolteacher before she became, in 1945, the first Latin American writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. Desolación, her first book, draws on grief as well as love, and she spent her life working for education across Latin America.
ML-205: This poem comes from the Shijing, or Book of Songs, China's oldest collection of poetry, gathered between about 1000 and 600 BCE. Tradition says Confucius chose its songs, and for two thousand years scholars read even its love songs as moral lessons.
ML-037: Julio Flórez was Colombia's most popular poet around 1900, a Romantic writing through the Thousand Days' War (1899–1902), which tore the country apart. His dark, emotional love poems were recited everywhere, and many, including this one, became popular songs.
ML-208: Hans Christian Andersen, now known for his fairy tales, also wrote poems. The young Norwegian composer Edvard Grieg set this one to music in 1864 for his cousin Nina Hagerup, whom he married in 1867, and it became one of Scandinavia's best-loved love songs.
ML-051: Medardo Ángel Silva grew up poor in Guayaquil and belonged to the 'beheaded generation' of young Ecuadorian poets who died early. He died in 1919 aged 21; this poem, later a famous pasillo song, is shadowed by the despair in his life.
ML-209: Runeberg wrote in Swedish, the language of Finland's educated class, soon after Finland passed from Swedish to Russian rule. He became Finland's national poet, and his words open the national anthem; this small lyric shows his gift for holding a single moment.
ML-210: Les Fleurs du Mal was prosecuted for offending public morals in 1857, and six of its poems stayed banned in France until 1949. Le Balcon is among the poems linked to Jeanne Duval, Baudelaire's partner for many years, a woman of mixed race whose own life is barely recorded.
ML-211: Heine's Buch der Lieder (1827) became one of the most popular poetry books of its century, and this poem was set to music by Schumann, Liszt and many others. Heine was born Jewish and later lived in exile in Paris; in 1933 the Nazis burned his books.
ML-213: Margit Kaffka was a pioneer of Hungarian modern writing and one of the first women in Hungary to make a living from writing. This poem stayed in manuscript and was published long after her death in the 1918 flu pandemic.
ML-214: Tagore translated this poem from his own Bengali, as he did for Gitanjali, the book that made him in 1913 the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. He wrote under British rule, and in 1919 gave up his British knighthood in protest at the Amritsar massacre.
ML-216: Yeats wrote this for Maud Gonne, the actor and revolutionary he loved for years and who turned down his proposals. It belongs to the Irish literary revival, when writers set out to build a national culture while Ireland was still under British rule.
ML-083: Rachel Bluwstein, known simply as Rachel, came from Russia to Ottoman Palestine in 1909 and worked on the land by the Sea of Galilee. Ill with tuberculosis, she wrote short, plain Hebrew poems that helped shape modern Hebrew verse, and died in 1931, before the state of Israel existed.
ML-217: This sonnet comes from the Vita nuova, Dante's account of his love for Beatrice, written in Florence in the 1290s. Writing about love in Italian rather than Latin was itself a bold choice; its best-known English translation is by the Victorian poet and painter Dante Gabriel Rossetti.
ML-085: Claude McKay grew up in rural Jamaica, then a British colony, and moved to the United States in 1912. Harlem Shadows (1922) helped launch the Harlem Renaissance, and his poems speak of love and beauty as well as protest against racism.
ML-218: Taira no Kanemori was a court poet of Heian Japan, where poems were part of courtship itself. This one won a famous poetry contest at the imperial palace in 960, and was later chosen for the Hyakunin Isshu, a hundred poems still used in a popular New Year card game.
ML-221: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz was a nun and scholar in colonial New Spain, now Mexico, and the most celebrated writer in the Spanish-speaking world of her time. She defended women's right to learn; whom she wrote her love poems for is still unknown.
ML-223: Katherine Mansfield left New Zealand for London at 19 and became one of the great short-story writers in English. She wrote this poem in 1916, months after her brother was killed in the First World War, and died of tuberculosis in 1923, aged 34.
ML-130: Henrik Ibsen, the playwright behind A Doll's House, began as a poet. Like most Norwegian writers of his day he wrote in the Danish-based written language left by four centuries of union with Denmark.
ML-227: Luís de Camões, Portugal's national poet, lived as a soldier and exile in Asia during the age of Portuguese voyages and empire. Legend says he swam ashore from a shipwreck holding the manuscript of his epic, The Lusiads; this sonnet is still learnt by heart in Portugal and Brazil.
ML-228: Mihai Eminescu is Romania's national poet, writing in the years when Romania won full independence in 1877–78. His own love life, above all his long and troubled affair with the poet Veronica Micle, runs through poems like this one.
ML-229: Pushkin wrote this in 1829, probably for Anna Olenina, who had turned down his proposal. He is Russia's national poet; his great-grandfather, Abram Gannibal, was an African brought to Russia as a captive child who rose to become a general.
ML-149: Robert Louis Stevenson settled in Samoa in 1890 and spent his last years there with his wife, Fanny. He sided with Samoans in their disputes with the colonial powers, Germany, Britain and the United States, and Samoans called him Tusitala, 'teller of tales'.
ML-159: France Prešeren is Slovenia's national poet, writing when Slovenia was part of the Austrian Empire. Much of his love poetry was for Julija Primic, who never returned his feelings; another of his poems is now Slovenia's national anthem.
ML-232: Bécquer's Rimas were gathered by friends and published in 1871, the year after his early death. Short, musical and personal, they broke with grand Romantic rhetoric and shaped modern poetry in Spanish; 'poetry is you' is among the most quoted lines in the language.
ML-233: Gustaf Fröding is one of Sweden's best-loved poets, and spent long periods in hospital with mental illness. In 1896 he was prosecuted, and acquitted, over a poem about sexuality; this poem comes from the same years, and is just as frank.
ML-234: Conrad Ferdinand Meyer of Zurich came to poetry late, after years of depression, and married Louise Ziegler in 1875. Zwei Segel, with its two sails moving as one, is often read as an image of that marriage.
ML-236: Lesya Ukrainka wrote when Ukraine was divided between the Russian and Austro-Hungarian empires, and printing in Ukrainian was restricted in Russia. She wrote this in 1900, while caring for Serhiy Merzhynsky, the man she loved, who was dying of tuberculosis.
ML-237: Shakespeare's sonnets were published in 1609, though many were probably written in the 1590s. Most of the first 126, including this one, are addressed to a young man; its promise that verse will outlast its subject has held for four centuries.
ML-238: Emily Dickinson wrote nearly 1,800 poems in Amherst, Massachusetts, but only about ten were published in her lifetime. Her first editors hesitated over printing this one in 1891 because of its passion; whom it was written for is still debated.
ML-239: Delmira Agustini published this poem at 20 and became one of the first women in Latin America to write openly about desire. In 1914 she was killed by her former husband, weeks after a divorce made possible by Uruguay's new divorce law.
